title: Planning Fallacy
hook: The plan feels shortest when you are standing at the start of it.
counterintuition: Your own plan is not special evidence; use the outside view and a premortem before the neat story becomes the schedule.
tryThisNow: Pick one plan you are sure will be quick. Write how long the last three similar jobs took, then add one failure that would explain a delay.
keyTakeaway: The planning fallacy makes the inside story feel cleaner than past evidence. Check similar cases before trusting your best-case path.

breakdown.fastRead: The waiting-list sheet in the diamond broker's office shows six buyers ahead of the new client. Juliet still wants to promise first offer by Friday because this stone feels easy to place. The planning fallacy turns a smooth story into a false schedule. She writes outside view on the sheet, checks the last ten first offers, and changes the promise to the real range.
breakdown.deepRead:
A plan is easiest to believe from the inside. You can see the clean path, the cooperative people, the smooth handoffs, and the version of yourself who starts early. The obstacles look like exceptions.

The planning fallacy is the error of using that inside story as if it were evidence. A language school expects level placement to take one day because this group looks straightforward. A food bank expects the trucks to load in two hours because the forecast grid looks tidy. A tenant team expects repairs to finish quickly because everyone agrees the complaints are urgent. The story may be sincere. It is still incomplete.

The outside view is the antidote.

Look at similar cases before you bless the plan. How long did the last ten placements take? Where did the last truck run slip? What broke in similar repairs? Then run a premortem: imagine the plan failed and list the plain reasons. The point is not to become grim. The point is to let past evidence compete with the tempting story.

This matters because early promises harden. A short schedule becomes a staffing plan, a budget, a public date, or a client expectation. Once that happens, reality has to fight the promise instead of informing it.
breakdown.fullRead:
The forecast grid in the food bank truck allocation looks calm. Linnea, the logistics lead, sees routes, pallets, drivers, and unloading windows arranged in neat blocks. Then the warehouse supervisor points to the last three holiday runs. Each one slipped after one donor truck arrived late. The inside story says this week can work. The outside view says the weak point has a record.

Planning fallacy is not just bad math. It is attachment to the plan's clean narrative. You imagine the task unfolding as intended, then treat interruptions as unlikely because they are not part of the picture. Past cases sit nearby, less vivid than the plan you are about to announce.

What happened the last time the work looked this simple?

Buehler, Griffin, and Ross studied optimistic time predictions from the inside of the planning fallacy. People often predict faster completion for their own tasks than past experience supports. Hofstadter's law turns the same pain into a joke: work takes longer than expected even when you account for that fact. Bent Flyvbjerg's work on large projects shows the public version, where plans can understate time and cost long before concrete is poured.

The practical move is to break the false inference: 'I can picture a smooth path, therefore this is a good estimate.' A smooth picture is only a picture. The estimate should come from a reference class, known bottlenecks, and a premortem that names how the plan might fail.

A plan without past cases is a wish with formatting.

A tenant-complaint meeting shows the pressure. Marek sees a donor pledge card for building repairs and wants to promise completion before the next inspection. Everyone in the room wants that promise to be true. If he uses the inside story, the date looks kind. If he marks the Flyvbjerg risk and compares similar repair jobs, the date becomes less pleasing and more useful.

The correction has three parts. First, state the plan in plain steps. Second, find the outside view: similar jobs, actual durations, known failure points, real staffing, and prior overruns. Third, run a premortem before the date is public. Ask why this plan failed, not to predict doom, but to expose hidden assumptions while they can still be changed.

The limit is that planning needs ambition. If you only copy the past, you may miss a genuine improvement. New tools, better staffing, smaller scope, or changed incentives can make this case different. But difference is a claim that needs evidence. Do not let uniqueness become a shelter for the best-case story.

Before the choice moves forward, make the outside view speak first. Put the last cases beside the new date. Put the premortem beside the launch promise. If the plan still holds, commit. If it shrinks under past evidence, be grateful that it shrank before the public promise did.

examples.title: Juliet checks the first-offer range
examples.scenario: A waiting-list sheet lies beside the diamond loupe in an Antwerp broker's office at 9:15 a.m. Juliet must decide whether to promise a first offer by Friday because the new stone feels easy to place. She marks planning fallacy on the sheet, checks the last ten first-offer dates with her assistant, and changes the promise to the real range.
examples.whatToDo: Use the last ten first-offer cases as the outside view before promising the client a date.
examples.whyItMatters: The stone's story feels smooth from the inside. Prior offers show the waiting list, buyer pauses, and paperwork delays.

planSpec.domain: a diamond broker first offer applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

examples.title: Raul places students by the old cases
examples.scenario: "This cohort looks easy," the director says during language school level placement in Madrid. Raul must decide whether to finish all placements in one day after glancing at a defect photo from last term's rushed test. He writes outside view on the photo, pulls last intake's placement times, and changes the schedule while the registrar watches.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the new cohort with the last intake's placement times before setting the one-day promise.
examples.whyItMatters: The group may look simple, but similar cohorts reveal testing delays, appeals, and retakes that the first glance hides.

planSpec.domain: a language school level placement applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

examples.title: Linnea runs the truck premortem
examples.scenario: The forecast grid smells of dry marker in the food bank dispatch room in Winnipeg at 6:40 a.m. Linnea, the route lead, must decide whether two trucks can cover five sites before noon. "Pretend it failed," she says, marking premortem beside the grid. The driver names late donor pallets, she adds a buffer route, and the truck allocation changes before keys are handed out.
examples.whatToDo: Use prior failed runs to price route slack before promising the delivery window.
examples.whyItMatters: The grid makes the day look tidy. The premortem forces known bottlenecks into the allocation before the trucks leave.

planSpec.domain: a food bank truck allocation applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

examples.title: Marek delays the neat repair promise
examples.scenario: You are holding a donor pledge card at 7:10 p.m. in a Warsaw tenant-complaint meeting, and the inspection date is already on the wall. Marek, the building manager, must choose between a pleasing repair promise and the last five repair durations. He writes Flyvbjerg on the card, asks the contractor for comparable jobs, and changes the pledge date in front of the tenants' representative.
examples.whatToDo: Put comparable repair jobs beside the pledge date before promising completion.
examples.whyItMatters: The desired date is kind but fragile. Similar repairs show permit lag, parts delays, and tenant access problems.

planSpec.domain: a tenant-complaint meeting applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

examples.title: Solveig tests the crash-hotspot timeline
examples.scenario: It took Solveig three crash-map updates in Oslo to see that the bike-share hotspot review kept trusting the cleanest repair path. At 5:25 p.m. in the transport office, Solveig, the safety analyst, sees the shift roster showing winter staffing had never matched the plan. Before publishing the fix date, she must decide whether Hofstadter's warning means adding the staffing record or repeating the short timeline.
examples.whatToDo: Anchor the repair date to winter staffing capacity before announcing the fix.
examples.whyItMatters: The map fix may be clear, but staff availability controls the date. The roster gives the outside view.

planSpec.domain: a bike-share crash hotspot review applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

examples.title: Esteban's bonus-test postmortem
examples.scenario: Which was wrong: the payroll bonus idea or the launch date? Esteban asks that after a Lisbon payroll bonus test misses its first payout cycle. At 9:30 a.m. in the finance review room, Esteban, the payroll lead, opens the risk register that had listed system changes as footnotes. He marks planning on the register and changes the next test so every listed risk gets a date owner before launch is announced.
examples.whatToDo: Turn risk-register items into dated owners before announcing the next bonus-test launch.
examples.whyItMatters: The plan did not fail because bonuses were impossible. It failed because known setup risks never entered the date.

planSpec.domain: a payroll bonus test applying Planning Fallacy under operational pressure

reviewCards.front: A new plan feels clean and quick. What reference class should anchor the estimate?
reviewCards.back: Use comparable past projects, not the inside story, to estimate time, cost, and friction.
Comparable past cases, real durations, common delays, staffing limits, and prior overruns.
Imagine the plan failed, then list the plain reasons while there is still time to change the plan.

reviewCards.front: When is this case really different?
reviewCards.back: When evidence shows the new tool, scope, staffing, or incentive changes the bottleneck that delayed past cases.
They harden into staffing, budgets, public dates, and client expectations before reality has been checked.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use the outside view and a premortem before turning the inside story into a public date.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a date feels easy, then I will check the last comparable cases before promising it.
If a grid looks tidy, then I will ask where the last similar run slipped.
If people want the kind date, then I will compare similar work before making it public.
If a risk appears in the register, then I will give it an owner and date before launch.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one plan with a date. Add the last three similar cases and one premortem reason before you share the date.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, compare a plan's original timeline with the outside view you should have used.
